title: The Ari
hookLine: Isaac Luria teaches in Safed for about two years and transforms Jewish mystical thought

cards: How long does it take to change the way a people prays? A lifetime, perhaps. A great book, a school, a long career.
Here's a teacher who, tradition says, spent only a short time in Tzfat before he died young. He wrote very little. He taught a small circle of students, out loud, on walks and at tables.
And yet the ideas they carried away shaped Jewish prayer books and mystical study, and some hear them in a phrase about fixing the world.

teach.b: His name was Rabbi Isaac Luria. Ari means lion in Hebrew, and tradition says the title also stands for the initials of a phrase meaning the godly Rabbi Isaac.
His teachings come to us mainly through a student, Chaim Vital, who wrote them down in a large work called Etz Chaim, the Tree of Life. At their heart is a story about creation, in three movements.
First, tzimtzum, contraction. How can there be a world at all, if God is everywhere? The Ari taught that God, as it were, drew back, making room.

Second, the breaking of the vessels. Divine light poured into vessels that could not hold it, and they shattered. Sparks of holiness fell and were scattered through the world, hidden in ordinary things.
Third, tikkun, repair. In this teaching, every prayer said with intention, every commandment done with care, lifts a spark and helps mend what broke.

Some historians, Gershom Scholem among them, see in it a story that matched the lives of the exiles from Spain: a world cracked open, holiness scattered like a people, and a task for each person to help put it back together.

It turned small acts into large ones. The phrase tikkun olam, repairing the world, is older than the Ari; it appears in the Mishnah and in the Aleinu prayer. Since his time it can carry an echo of this teaching.
A psalm asks for the wisdom of a short life: "So teach us to number our days, that we may get us a heart of wisdom." The lion taught briefly. The roar carried.

how: Some Jews study the Ari's teachings in Kabbalah circles, and some prayer books, especially in Hasidic and Sephardic communities, follow customs and intentions drawn from his school.

games.q: you are one of the Ari's students. he teaches out loud and writes almost nothing. what do you do?
o: remember what you can and move on.
games.why: Chaim Vital wrote the teachings down in Etz Chaim, the Tree of Life, which is how they reach us.

practice: Call to mind something short that changed you: a sentence a teacher once said, a friend you knew for only a few months, a single conversation with a stranger.
Let the shortness of it sit beside the size of what it gave, and if you pray, say the psalm's line: teach us to number our days.

wordCard.voice: The Ari. Rabbi Isaac Luria of Tzfat, the lion, who taught contraction, the breaking of the vessels, and repair, and whose students carried those ideas into Jewish prayer and thought. Today's word.

orig.note: ari is Hebrew for lion; tradition also reads it as initials.

carryVoice: Your line: the lion. In his teaching, small acts done with care lift hidden sparks. See you tomorrow.
